To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cerebral cortex is generated by the inside‐to‐out sequence of cell production, that the fate of a cell born at a specific time is not determined by its birthdate alone, and that the nervous system is plastic enough to compensate to some degree for the loss of specific sets of progenitors.

(1) the cerebral cortex develops in an inside‐to‐outside sequence, with the deep cortical layers being born first and the superficial layers last; (2) the destruction of cortical precursors at E12 results in a thinning of the cerebral cortex, but all cortical layers are present and have normal connections; and (3) the destruction of precursors at E10 results in a normal‐appearing cortex, but many superficial cortical cells are abnormally deep.

the cerebral cortex is generated in an inside‐to‐out sequence and that, after destruction of specific cortical precursor cells with MAM Ac, the remaining progenitor cells can compensate to some extent, but not completely, for the missing cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the cerebral cortex forms.
the cellular events that occur as the nervous system is generated.
how the cerebral cortex develops, and how it is able to recover from damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the embryonic age of a cell is a major but not the sole factor that determines the ultimate position and connections of that cell in the mature cerebral cortex.

, during the period of cortical cell production, the nervous system has a high degree of plasticity, which is reflected in the fact that it can compensate to some extent, by altering the fotes of later‐produced cells, for the destruction of earlier‐produced ones.
the cerebral cortex is generated in an inside‐to‐outside sequence from E12 to E16, with the superficial layers being produced last.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cortex is a mosaic of cells born at different times, and that these cells are not necessarily committed to specific fates at birth.
, during the period of neurogenesis, cortical progenitors are not irreversibly committed to their ultimate fate.
the fate of a cortical cell is not fixed at the moment of its birth, but is instead determined by a combination of intrinsic factors and extrinsic cues that are present at the time of its birth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a great deal of flexibility in how the brain is put together.
, in the developing cerebral cortex, the date of birth is a poor predictor of the fate of a cell.
the cerebral cortex is a dynamic structure that is capable of compensating for the destruction of a significant fraction of its progenitor population.
